label: root_cause_decision_false_positive
content:
[user]: what was the root cause?
[assistant]: The generic problem is: completion confirmations are being misread as decisions by the extraction LLM. The model sees 'rename + threshold + prompt...' in a commit message and treats it as a choice, not a report. This class includes git pushes, deployments, and test run completions. The decision extraction prompt needs explicit guidance that completed actions reported after the fact are NOT decisions — a decision requires deliberation between alternatives.
[user]: how did we fix it?
[assistant]: Added two rules to the prompt: (1) REJECT retrospective completion reports that only describe fixing without naming a chosen approach, and (2) require decision_evidence_text to contain an actual decision cue phrase, not just implementation narration.

label: memory_quality_structural_analysis
content:
[user]: so what changed in terms of quality?

The root problem was that short, immediate questions like 'how do I know if pallium brings value?' were being classified as durable interest memories. Now: structural gate ensures sources with < 10 tokens can never produce interest memories regardless of LLM output. Production data showed 8 genuine false positives — every single one was a short question asking for immediate help.
[user]: can we proove we improved quality/
[assistant]: Yes. The dry-run identifies 8 interest memories that are genuine false positives. Every single one is a short question asking for immediate help. The token gate catches all 8.

label: discussion_summary_architecture
content:
[user]: about discussion summary - it looks like they only contain only a single message. is that the case?
[assistant]: That's the key finding. discussion_summary (now turn_summary) is always a per-item fallback type. When the write extraction prompt produces candidate_type=null for a source item, and the item has enough substance to not be is_low_value_meta, it becomes a turn_summary. It's NOT a thread-level aggregation — each one corresponds to exactly one source item. The thread_summary type is the aggregated one, but that's separate and uses its own prompt.

label: subprocess_logging_discovery
content:
[user]: why don't i see errors in the log file?
[assistant]: The log file uses RotatingFileHandler — it rotates at 5MB with 5 backups, so max ~30MB total on disk. That's configured in runtime_logging.py:79-81. However, there's a child-process logging issue: subprocess logs aren't captured by the parent handler because each subprocess has its own Python interpreter and logging context. They write to stderr instead. This means background worker errors are lost unless explicitly redirected to the parent's log file.

label: race_condition_root_cause_and_fix
content:
[user]: items are getting processed twice sometimes
[assistant]: Found it. claim_next_source_item only checks the source_items status column and had no awareness of the package table. When two packages run concurrently, both can claim the same item because the status update and package creation aren't atomic. SQL race condition fix: added a NOT EXISTS subquery to the legacy claim SQL that skips items with active package_processing rows. This eliminates the double-processing window.
[user]: is this something that we should test?
[assistant]: Yes — added a concurrent-claim test that spawns two workers and verifies only one gets the item. The test uses threading to simulate the race window.

label: hf_hub_offline_discovery
content:
[user]: embedding loads hang for 60 seconds under rate limiting
[assistant]: The issue is HuggingFace Hub freshness checks. On every model load, the HF client checks if a newer version exists on the hub. Under rate limiting (HTTP 429), this check blocks for 60 seconds waiting for the retry. Fix: set HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 in the environment. This tells the HF client to use only the local cache without any network calls. It affects all embedding model loads but since we pin model versions anyway, there's no downside.
[user]: make sure this is set in the service install
[assistant]: Added HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 to the environment variables in both the scheduled task definition and the systemd service unit.

label: fts5_migration_decision
content:
[user]: the lexical search is too slow on large datasets
[assistant]: Confirmed — the current implementation does a full table scan with Python-side IDF scoring. That's O(N) per query. For the 1000+ memory objects we have now, it's already taking 200ms+. I've switched to FTS5 which gives us inverted-index lookup with BM25 scoring at millisecond latency regardless of corpus size. The migration script rebuilds the FTS index from existing memory objects.
[user]: and the old approach is completely removed?
[assistant]: Yes — removed the full-scan code path entirely. FTS5 is now the only lexical backend. The old sqlite_search.py scan function is deleted.

label: visibility_filter_architecture
content:
[user]: but why in the screnshot i gave you i queried with public and still gor memories?
[assistant]: That's because the visibility filter works differently than you'd expect. When you query with visibility='public', it returns memories that are visible TO the public scope — which includes memories explicitly marked 'public' AND memories from shared containers. The private memories from your personal container are filtered out, but the container git:github.com/rore/pallium is a shared container, so its memories show up in both public and private queries.
[user]: wait, but isn't the claude integration ingests all as private?
[assistant]: Yes — the Claude Code integration sets visibility='private' on every ingested item. But the container itself determines sharing scope. Private visibility means only the actor who created it can see it in OTHER containers. In the same container, all items are visible to all actors.
